title: Water Margin
description: One of the Chinese Classic Novels
wiki_lead:
Water Margin (simplified Chinese: 水浒传; traditional Chinese: 水滸傳; pinyin: Shuǐhǔ Zhuàn), also called Outlaws of the Marsh or All Men Are Brothers, is a Chinese novel from the Ming dynasty, attributed to Shi Nai'an. Regarded as one of the greatest Chinese novels, the novel is among the first works of Chinese fiction written entirely in vernacular Chinese. It is considered a masterpiece of Chinese literature, as well as a book of heroism and transgression.
Set during the Northern Song dynasty (twelfth century), the story follows a group of 108 outlaws that gathers at Mount Liang (also known as Liangshan Marsh) to rebel against the government. Later they are granted amnesty and enlisted by the government to resist the nomadic conquest of the Liao dynasty and other rebels. The original title of the novel was Water Margin for Loyalty and Justice (忠義水滸傳). A wealth of bibliographical and other evidence names Shi Nai'an, Luo Guanzhong (fl. 1330–1400), or both of them, as the novel's principal compiler, responsible for its original compilation. Through a complex textual evolution, a printed revision based on previous editions was published during the reign of Emperor Shizong (1522–1566) of the Ming dynasty, becoming the ancestral edition to a series of the most widely circulated versions. Dealing with social critique, the novel explores themes of morality, justice, authority and loyalty, and has been banned many times in its history.
Water Margin is an immediate inspiration for the later vernacular novels in its language, narrative rhetoric, structure, and distinctive elaboration of the themes of martiality and chivalry. The critics Li Zhi and Jin Shengtan both placed the book among the "greatest works of genius" in Chinese literature, and modern scholars and critics have been nearly unanimous in their praise of the work. Known for its heroic characterization of vigilantes, outlaws, and others who resist authority, the novel has introduced readers to some of the best-known characters in Chinese literature, such as Shi Jin, Lu Zhishen, Lin Chong, Wu Song, Li Kui, Yan Qing and Song Jiang. Its characters and plots frequently reappear in other novels, operas, and performance media of all sorts. With its theme of righteous bandit rebellion, Water Margin has long been an allegorical tool of historical and political commentary. Its influence spread far beyond the confines of literature.

Historical context and inspirations
Water Margin is based on the exploits of the outlaw Song Jiang and his 107 companions; framed in the story as the incarnations of 108 demons representing 108 stars (the “36 heavenly spirits" (三十六天罡; sānshíliù tiāngāng) and the “72 earthly demons" (七十二地煞; qīshíèr dìshā)). The activities of Song Jiang's group were recorded in the historical text History of Song in the annals of Emperor Huizong of Song, which states:

(When) the outlaw Song Jiang of Huainan and others attacked the army at Huaiyang, (the Emperor) sent generals to attack and arrest them. (The outlaws) infringed on the east of the capital (Kaifeng), Henan, and entered the boundaries of Chu (referring to present-day Hubei and Hunan) and Haizhou (covering parts of present-day Jiangsu). The general Zhang Shuye was ordered to pacify them.
Zhang Shuye's biography further describes the activities of Song Jiang and the other outlaws, and tells they were eventually defeated by Zhang.

Folk stories about Song Jiang circulated during the Southern Song, and Song Jiang came to be portrayed as a rebel leader, fighting against their enemy, the Jin. The first known source to name Song Jiang's 36 companions was Miscellaneous Observations from the Year of Guixin (癸辛雜識) by Zhou Mi, written in the 13th century. Among the 36 of Song Jiang's companions, there are names like Lu Junyi, Guan Sheng, Ruan Xiao'er, Ruan Xiaowu, Ruan Xiaoqi, Liu Tang, Hua Rong and Wu Yong. The narrative, drawing from oral traditions and historical accounts of banditry in the late Northern Song dynasty (circa 1120 CE), recounts how a disparate group of 108 marginalized heroesâeach endowed with supernatural destinies as indicated by a prophetic stone tabletâconverge at the Liangshan Marshes to form a formidable outlaw brotherhood under the leadership of Song Jiang, resisting extortionate officials and imperial malfeasance through guerrilla warfare and chivalric feats. As one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature, Water Margin pioneered the extended prose fiction form in the vernacular language, emphasizing themes of yi (righteous brotherhood), anti-corruption rebellion, and the tension between personal loyalty and state authority, profoundly shaping subsequent depictions of heroism and social dissent in East Asian culture. The outlaws' arc culminates in their acceptance of amnesty from the imperial court, transforming into a loyalist army that crushes Liao dynasty invaders but meets tragic ends in futile campaigns, underscoring the causal perils of compromising principled insurgency for institutional reintegration. Its compilation reflects Ming-era synthesis of Song-Yuan storytelling cycles, with the fullest versions circulating by the 16th century, influencing myriad adaptations in opera, woodblock prints, and modern media while embodying a realist critique of bureaucratic decay over idealized Confucian harmony.
